We do not know f, and we do not need to. Think of f minus 9 as one even number, and walk forward from it.

ask.ifNot: Even and odd numbers take turns. So the number right next to it, 1 more, is odd.

So the 1st one is 1 more. After that, each new odd number is 2 further on: 3 away, then 5 away.
To get from the 1st to the 25th takes 24 more jumps of 2. Careful: 24 jumps, not 25, because the 1st one is already counted.
24 jumps of 2 cover 48. Add the first step of 1, and we have gone 49 in all.
So the 25th odd number is 49 more than our starting number, f minus 9.
Minus 9 and plus 49 together make plus 40. So we have f plus 40.
Try it with a real number. If f is 11, then f minus 9 is 2. Going on by 49 lands on 51. And 11 plus 40 is 51 too.
So the answer is f plus 40. Remember: 1 step to reach the first one, then jumps of 2 for all the rest.

ask.ifNot: Even and odd numbers take turns. So the number right next to it, 1 more, is odd.

beats.say: What is the first odd number after any even number?
So the 1st one is 1 more. After that, each new odd number is 2 further on: 3 away, then 5 away.
To get from the 1st to the 17th takes 16 more jumps of 2. Careful: 16 jumps, not 17, because the 1st one is already counted.
16 jumps of 2 cover 32. Add the first step of 1, and we have gone 33 in all.
So the 17th odd number is 33 more than our starting number, x plus 37.
Plus 37 and plus 33 together make plus 70. So we have x plus 70.
Try it with a real number. If x is 1, then x plus 37 is 38. Going on by 33 lands on 71. And 1 plus 70 is 71 too.
So the answer is x plus 70. Remember: 1 step to reach the first one, then jumps of 2 for all the rest.
We want the greatest odd number that uses 7, 5, 2, 0 and 4, each once.
For the greatest number we would love to write the digits biggest first. That gives 75420. But it ends in 0, so it is even. Not allowed!

ask.ifNot: The 7 is our biggest digit, so it is worth far more at the front. We spend the smaller odd digit, 5, on the units place.

beats.say: An odd number needs an odd digit at the end. Our odd digits are 7 and 5. Which one should go last?
Keep 7 in front, put 5 at the end, and arrange what is left, 4, 2 and 0, biggest first. That makes 74205.
Compare it with putting 7 at the end. The best we could do then is 54207, and 74205 is far greater.
And it really is odd, because it ends in 5.
So the greatest odd number is 74205.
Decide the last digit first, using the smaller odd digit. Then put the others in order, biggest first.
Four numbers. In one of them, the tens digit is exactly four times the thousands digit.
In a 4 digit number the thousands digit is the first one, and the tens digit is the third one. Here they are in 8621.
Think before testing. If the thousands digit is 8, four times it is 32, and that is not a single digit. So both numbers starting with 8 are out.

ask.ifNot: Four times the thousands digit: 4 times 2 is 8. So we need an 8 in the tens place.

beats.say: Now 2386. Its thousands digit is 2. So what must its tens digit be?
4 times 2 is 8, and the tens digit of 2386 really is 8. It fits!
Check the last one, 4538. 4 times 4 is 16, but its tens digit is 3. Out.
So the number is 2386.
Name the places first. Then test each number, and use what you know to rule some out quickly.
Here is 43541. We are going to slip a 2 in between the 3 and the 5.
The 4 and the 3 stay in front, then comes the new 2, then 5, 4, 1. That makes 432541.

choices: they moved one place to the left
they moved one place to the right
they stayed in the same places
ask.ifNot: The number grew from 5 digits to 6. So the front digits were pushed one column to the left, where they are worth 10 times more.

beats.say: What happened to the 4 and the 3 at the front when the 2 squeezed in?
In the new number the 4 is in the lakhs place, and the 3 is in the ten-thousands place. They are worth far more now.
To find how much more the new number is, subtract the old from the new. The last three digits are the same in both, so they cancel to zeros.
Check by adding back: 43541 plus 389000 is 432541.
So the new number is more by 389000. That is far more than the new 2 is worth, because the 4 and the 3 moved as well.
When a digit is slipped in, every digit to its left jumps one column. Subtract the whole numbers to see the full change.
A palindrome reads the same both ways, like 707. We add a 3 digit palindrome to 2017 and get a 4 digit palindrome.

board.text: the number looks like:  a b a

beats.say: Our 3 digit palindrome has the same first and last digit. And 2017 plus a 3 digit number should still start with 2, so the answer must end in 2 as well.

ask.ifNot: 7 plus 5 makes a ten and 2 more, so it ends in 2. No other single digit does that.

beats.say: Look at the units. 7 plus our last digit must end in 2. Which digit does that?
7 plus 5 is 12. So the last digit is 5, and because it is a palindrome, the first digit is 5 too.
Now the middle digit. Try 0 in the middle first: 2017 plus 505 is 2522. Not a palindrome yet.
Each time the middle digit goes up by 1, the total goes up by 10: 2522, 2532, 2542, 2552. Stop! 2552 reads the same backwards.
We went up 3 steps, so the middle digit is 3. The number is 535, and 2017 plus 535 is 2552.
The question wants the digit sum of 535. 5 plus 3 plus 5 is 13.
So the answer is 13. Start from the units digit, because that is where a sum begins.
First we build the greatest 5 digit number from 9, 5, 0, 7 and 3. Then we compare what its 5 and its 3 are worth.

ask.ifNot: The places on the left are worth the most. So the biggest digits should go there, in order.

beats.say: To make the greatest number, how do we arrange the digits?
9, 7, 5, 3, 0. The greatest number is 97530.
The 5 has landed in the hundreds place. 5 times 100 is 500.
The 3 is in the tens place. 3 times 10 is 30.
Difference means subtract. Careful: we subtract the place values, not the digits. 500 minus 30 is 470.
So the difference is 470.
Build the number, find each place value, then subtract. Three small steps, in that order.

board.text: (x + 37) is even. The 17th odd number before it?

We do not know x, and we do not need to. Think of x plus 37 as one even number, and walk backwards from it.

ask.ifNot: Even and odd numbers take turns. So the number right next to it, 1 less, is odd.

beats.say: What is the first odd number before any even number?
So the 1st one is 1 less. After that, each new odd number is 2 further back: 3 away, then 5 away.
To get from the 1st to the 17th takes 16 more jumps of 2. Careful: 16 jumps, not 17, because the 1st one is already counted.
16 jumps of 2 cover 32. Add the first step of 1, and we have gone 33 in all.
So the 17th odd number is 33 less than our starting number, x plus 37.
Plus 37, then minus 33, leaves plus 4. So we have x plus 4.
Try it with a real number. If x is 3, then x plus 37 is 40. Going back by 33 lands on 7. And 3 plus 4 is 7 too.
So the answer is x plus 4. Remember: 1 step to reach the first one, then jumps of 2 for all the rest.
We want the 27th even number that comes after 27.

ask.ifNot: Odd and even numbers take turns. One more than 27 is 28, and 28 is even.

beats.say: 27 is odd. So what is the first even number after it?
So the list starts 28, 30, 32, 34 and carries on in jumps of 2.
28 is the 1st. To reach the 27th we need 26 more jumps. Careful: 26, not 27, because 28 itself is already counted.
26 jumps of 2 cover 52.
28 plus 52 is 80.
A quick test of the method on a small case: the 2nd even number should be 28 plus 1 jump, which is 30. Yes, it is.
So the 27th even number after 27 is 80. Find the first one, then add one jump fewer than the position.

board.text: digits 2, 3, 4, 5: numbers with 5 in the hundreds

beats.say: All the 4 digit numbers made from 2, 3, 4 and 5, each used once. In how many is the 5 in the hundreds place?
Let's pin the 5 where it has to be. The hundreds place is taken, and three places are still empty.

ask.ifNot: Each digit is used only once, and the 5 is already taken. So only 2, 3 and 4 are left.

beats.say: Which digits are left to fill the empty places?
For the thousands place we can pick any of the 3. Then 2 are left for the tens, and 1 for the units.
Let's list them: 2534, 2543, 3524, 3542, 4523, 4532. Every one has 5 in the hundreds place.
So there are 6 such numbers.
Pin down the place that is decided. Then count the choices for the others and multiply.
Here is 75003064. We may shuffle its digits any way we like, to make the smallest number we can.
First sort the digits from smallest to biggest. There are three zeros, then 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7.

choices: No, it would lose a digit
ask.ifNot: A zero at the front is never written, so the number would become shorter. We need the smallest digit that is not zero.

beats.say: The smallest digit is 0. Can our number start with 0?
So 3 goes first.
Now the zeros are welcome. They go straight after the 3, in the biggest places left, where they keep the number small.
Then the rest in rising order: 4, 5, 6, 7. That makes 30004567.
Careful: 30405067 also starts with 3, but it spends a 4 in the lakhs place where a 0 could go. Ours is smaller.
So the smallest number is 30004567. Smallest digit that is not zero first, then the zeros, then the rest in order.
Here is 87459. We compare what the 7 is worth with what the 5 is worth.

ask.ifNot: Count from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands. So the 7 means 7 thousands.

beats.say: Find them in the chart. What is the 7 worth?
7 times 1000 is 7000. And the 5 is in the tens place, so it is worth 5 times 10, which is 50.

ask.ifNot: 1000 divided by 10 compares the columns only, and forgets the digits 7 and 5. We divide the full place values.

beats.say: 'How many times' is which sum?
7000 divided by 50. Cross a zero off each to make it easier: 700 divided by 5 is 140.
Check: 140 times 50 gives back 7000.
So the place value of the 7 is 140 times the place value of the 5.
The digits are different here, so comparing the columns alone is not enough. Always divide the full place values.

board.text: (x + 21) is odd. The 3rd even number after it?

beats.say: There is a letter in this one, but it is really a counting puzzle.
We do not know x, but we do know x plus 21 is odd. Let's walk forward from it, one number at a time.

ask.ifNot: Odd and even numbers take turns, like left foot, right foot. After an odd number comes an even one.

beats.say: What kind of number comes right after an odd number?
So the 1st even number is just 1 more: x plus 22.
Even numbers are 2 apart. So the 2nd one is x plus 24.
And the 3rd is x plus 26. Careful: the first step was only 1, because we started on an odd number. After that the steps are 2.
Try it with a real number. If x is 2, then x plus 21 is 23. The even numbers after 23 are 24, 26, 28. And 2 plus 26 is 28.
So the answer is x plus 26. One step to reach the first even number, then jumps of 2.

board.text: place value of 9 − place value of 7 = 83000

beats.say: Four numbers, each with a 9 and a 7. In one of them, the place values of the 9 and the 7 differ by 83000.

ask.ifNot: Try them. 90000 minus 7000 is 83000. The other pairs give differences that are too small or too big.

beats.say: Think first. Which two place values have a difference of 83000?
90000 minus 7000 is 83000. So the 9 must be worth 90000 and the 7 must be worth 7000.
That means 9 in the ten-thousands place, with 7 right beside it in the thousands place. Let's look for that pattern.
1907000: here the 9 is in the lakhs place, worth 900000. Far too much.
109700: the 9 is only worth 9000. And in 91700 the 9 is right, but the 7 is only worth 700. Both out.
197000: 9 in the ten-thousands, 7 in the thousands. Exactly what we wanted.
So the number is 197000. Working out what we needed first made the search quick.

board.text: two primes next to each other add up to 42

beats.say: Two prime numbers, next to each other in the list of primes, add up to 42. We want the difference between them.
If two numbers are close together and add up to 42, each must be close to half of 42. Half of 42 is 21.

ask.ifNot: 20 is even, so it is not prime. 19 cannot be divided by anything, so it is the nearest prime below 21.

beats.say: So one prime is a little below 21 and the other a little above. Which is the nearest prime below 21?
Here are the numbers around 21. Cross out 20 and 22, which are even, and 21, which is 3 times 7. The primes left are 19 and 23.
19 plus 23 is 42. It fits! And there is no prime between them, so they really are next to each other.
Now the difference. 23 minus 19 is 4.
So the two primes differ by 4.
When two numbers have a known total, start from half of it and look on both sides.

board.text: three numbers in a row add up to 66

beats.say: Three numbers in a row add up to 66. We need to find them, then see which one is among the choices.
Three numbers in a row are balanced around the middle one. One is 1 less, one is 1 more. So together they equal 3 lots of the middle number.

ask.ifNot: Three equal lots make 66. To find one lot, we share 66 into 3 equal parts.

beats.say: So how do we find the middle number?
66 divided by 3 is 22. That is the middle number.
One less is 21, and one more is 23. So the numbers are 21, 22 and 23.
Check by adding: 21 plus 22 plus 23 is 66.
Of our three numbers, the one offered in the choices is 23.
For numbers in a row, divide the total by how many there are. That gives the middle one.

board.text: page numbers use 555 digits. How many pages?

beats.say: Jack's book uses 555 digits for its page numbers. We work backwards to find how many pages there are.
Let's spend the 555 digits group by group. Pages 1 to 9 use 1 digit each. That is 9 digits.

ask.ifNot: From 1 to 99 there are 99 pages. Take away the first 9, and 90 pages are left.

beats.say: Next, the pages with 2 digits, from 10 up to 99. How many pages is that?
90 pages times 2 digits is 180. With the first 9, we have used 189 digits by page 99.
555 minus 189 leaves 366 digits for the pages with 3 digits.
Careful: 366 is a number of digits, not pages. Each of these pages takes 3 digits, and 366 divided by 3 is 122 pages.
99 pages before, plus 122 more, makes 221.
So Jack's book has 221 pages. Use up the 1 digit and 2 digit pages first, then share what is left among the 3 digit pages.
Which of these four numbers can be divided exactly by 11? Dividing each one would take ages, so we use a test.
Here is the test for 11. Add every other digit, starting with the first. Then add the digits you skipped. Take one total from the other.
If that difference is 0, or 11, or another multiple of 11, the number can be divided by 11.
Try 3116365. Every other digit: 3, 1, 3, 5, which make 12. The skipped ones: 1, 6, 6, which make 13. The difference is only 1. Out.

ask.ifNot: 9 plus 1 is 10, and 5 more makes 15.

beats.say: Now 901351. Every other digit: 9, 1 and 5. What do they add up to?
15 for those. The skipped digits, 0, 3 and 1, make 4. And 15 minus 4 is 11. That passes the test!
A quick look at the others. 11111 gives 3 and 2, a difference of 1. 8790321 gives 21 and 9, a difference of 12. Both out.
So the number is 901351. For 11: add alternate digits, subtract the two totals, and look for 0 or a multiple of 11.
Each of these numbers has two 6s. In only one of them is one 6 worth 1000 times the other.

ask.ifNot: One column is times 10. Every extra column is times 10 again. It takes three of them to make 1000, so we need 3 columns.

beats.say: Moving a digit one column to the left makes it worth 10 times more. To be worth 1000 times more, how many columns must it move?
So we look for two 6s with a gap of 3 columns. In 66728 the 6s are neighbours. A gap of 1.
In 68726 one 6 is in the ten-thousands and the other in the units. A gap of 4. Too wide.
In 86762 they are in the thousands and the tens. A gap of 2. Not enough.
In 68762 they are in the ten-thousands and the tens. A gap of 3. That is the one!
Check with the real values: 60000 and 60. 60000 divided by 60 is 1000.
So the number is 68762. With the same digit, count the columns between them: each column is one more times 10.
A number made only of 4s, like 444, that can be divided exactly by 18. What is the fewest 4s it can have?
18 is 2 times 9. So our number must be divisible by 2, and also by 9.
Divisible by 2 is easy. The number ends in 4, which is even. So that part is always fine.

choices: the digit sum is a multiple of 9
ask.ifNot: For 9, we add up all the digits. If that total is in the 9 times table, the number can be divided by 9.

beats.say: Now the 9. What is the test for dividing by 9?
Every digit is a 4, so the digit sum climbs in fours. We need the first total that is also in the 9 times table.
36 is the first one. It is 4 times 9, so it takes 9 fours to get there.
So the smallest such number has 9 fours.
Split 18 into 2 and 9, and test each one. The 2 was free, and the 9 test did all the work.

board.text: (Z + 41) is even. The 19th odd number before it?

beats.say: This one looks like algebra, but it is really about counting along a line of numbers.
We do not know Z, and we do not need to. Think of Z plus 41 as one even number, and walk backwards from it.

ask.ifNot: Even and odd numbers take turns. So the number right next to it, 1 less, is odd.

beats.say: What is the first odd number before any even number?
So the 1st one is 1 less. After that, each new odd number is 2 further back: 3 away, then 5 away.
To get from the 1st to the 19th takes 18 more jumps of 2. Careful: 18 jumps, not 19, because the 1st one is already counted.
18 jumps of 2 cover 36. Add the first step of 1, and we have gone 37 in all.
So the 19th odd number is 37 less than our starting number, Z plus 41.
Plus 41, then minus 37, leaves plus 4. So we have Z plus 4.
Try it with a real number. If Z is 1, then Z plus 41 is 42. Going back by 37 lands on 5. And 1 plus 4 is 5 too.
So the answer is Z plus 4. Remember: 1 step to reach the first one, then jumps of 2 for all the rest.
A square number is a number times itself. We are counting the squares that have 3 digits and are odd.
First, which squares have 3 digits? 10 times 10 is 100, the smallest 3 digit number. So we start at 10.
31 times 31 is 961, still 3 digits. But 32 times 32 is 1024, which is too long. So we stop at 31.

ask.ifNot: Odd times odd is odd, and even times even is even. So only an odd number has an odd square.

beats.say: Now, which numbers give an odd square?
So we need the odd numbers from 10 to 31. Here they are, starting at 11 and ending at 31.
Count along the list and you will find 11 numbers. Each one gives an odd square, so there are 11 odd squares with 3 digits.
Now look at the choices: 10, 12 and 13. Our 11 is not there!
So the answer is 'None of these'. Trust your working: when your number is not on the list, that is the right choice.
The number is given in words: sixty-seven lakhs, ninety-four thousand, five hundred and twenty-one. First we turn it into digits.
In the Indian system we write it with commas like this: 67 for the lakhs, 94 for the thousands, then the last three digits.

ask.ifNot: Count them one by one: 6, 7, 9, 4, 5, 2, 1. That is 7 digits.

beats.say: How many digits does the number have?
7 digits, so the middle one is the 4th, with 3 digits on each side of it. That is the 4.
Now, which column is the 4 in? Units, tens, hundreds, thousands. It is in the thousands place.
4 thousands: 4 times 1000 is 4000.
Careful: the 9 beside it is in the ten-thousands place. They are neighbours, so it is easy to mix them up.
So the place value is 4000. Write the number in digits first, find the middle, then name its column.
Five numbers. We keep only the ones that 3 divides exactly, and then add those up.

ask.ifNot: For 3, the last digit does not help. Add up the digits: if the total is in the 3 times table, so is the number.

beats.say: What is the quick test for dividing by 3?
861: 8 plus 6 plus 1 is 15. 435: 4 plus 3 plus 5 is 12. Both totals are in the 3 times table, so we keep both.
218 gives 11, and 764 gives 17. Neither is a multiple of 3, so cross them out.
1263 gives 12. Keep it.
Now add the three we kept. 861 plus 435 is 1296. Then 1296 plus 1263 is 2559.
So the sum is 2559.
Test with the digit sum, keep the ones that pass, then add. Sorting first keeps the adding small.

board.text: (M + 46) is a 2-digit prime. The 19th even number before it?

beats.say: A letter in the question, but no need to worry. This is a counting puzzle in disguise.
First, a clue to decode. A prime with 2 digits cannot be even, because the only even prime is 2. So M plus 46 is an odd number.
We do not know M, and we do not need to. Think of M plus 46 as one odd number, and walk backwards from it.

ask.ifNot: Even and odd numbers take turns. So the number right next to it, 1 less, is even.

beats.say: What is the first even number before any odd number?
So the 1st one is 1 less. After that, each new even number is 2 further back: 3 away, then 5 away.
To get from the 1st to the 19th takes 18 more jumps of 2. Careful: 18 jumps, not 19, because the 1st one is already counted.
18 jumps of 2 cover 36. Add the first step of 1, and we have gone 37 in all.
So the 19th even number is 37 less than our starting number, M plus 46.
Plus 46, then minus 37, leaves plus 9. So we have M plus 9.
Try it with a real number. If M is 1, then M plus 46 is 47. Going back by 37 lands on 10. And 1 plus 9 is 10 too.
So the answer is M plus 9. Remember: 1 step to reach the first one, then jumps of 2 for all the rest.
We want every one digit factor of 48, all multiplied together. A factor of 48 is a number that divides 48 exactly.
Let's test each one digit number, 1 to 9.

ask.ifNot: 48 does not end in 0 or 5, so 5 does not divide it. But 6 times 8 is 48, so 6 and 8 both do.

beats.say: Which of these does not divide 48?
5, 7 and 9 do not divide 48, so cross them out. The factors left are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8.
Now multiply them, in friendly groups. 1 times 2 times 3 times 4 is 24. And 6 times 8 is 48.
So we need 24 times 48. 24 times 50 is 1200. That is 2 lots of 24 too many, so take away 48. We get 1152.
So the product is 1152.
List, test, cross out, then multiply in easy groups. And notice the 1: it is a factor, but it changes nothing.
Three steps: find two special numbers, multiply them, then find what the 6 in the answer is worth.
The greatest 3 digit number is easy. It is 999.

ask.ifNot: 99 can be divided by 9, and 91 can be divided by 7. 97 cannot be divided by anything, so it is the greatest 2 digit prime.

beats.say: Now the greatest 2 digit prime. Which is it?
So we need 97 times 999.
999 is just 1 less than 1000. So take 97 thousands, and then take away one 97. That leaves 96903.
Now find the 6 in 96903. Units, tens, hundreds, thousands. It is in the thousands place.
6 thousands: 6 times 1000 is 6000.
So the place value of the 6 is 6000. Multiplying by 999 is easy when you think of it as 1000 take away 1.
We build the smallest 5 digit even number from 7, 4, 3, 6 and 9. Then we read off its hundreds digit.
Even means it ends in an even digit. Ours are 4 and 6, so one of them goes last.

ask.ifNot: If 4 went last, we could not use it near the front, where it keeps the number small. So we save the 4 and put 6 at the end.

beats.say: The smallest digit, 3, goes first. We would like 4 to come next. So which even digit should go last?
3, then 4, then 7 and 9 in rising order, and 6 at the end. That makes 34796.
Compare it with putting 4 at the end. The best we could do then is 36794, and ours is smaller.
Now the hundreds place. Units, tens, hundreds: the third digit from the right is 7.
So the digit in the hundreds place is 7.
Choose the last digit so that the small digits stay free for the front. Then count the places from the right.

board.text: (7th odd number after 54) + (12th even number before 65)

beats.say: Two little hunts, then one addition. First the 7th odd number after 54, then the 12th even number before 65.
The odd numbers after 54 are short enough to list: 55, 57, 59, 61, 63, 65, 67. The 7th one is 67.
Now the even numbers before 65. Counting backwards, they start at 64 and go down in jumps of 2.

ask.ifNot: The 1st is already there with no jump at all. Each jump after that gives one more, so the 12th needs 11 jumps.

beats.say: 64 is the 1st. How many jumps back do we need to reach the 12th?
11 jumps of 2 is 22. And 64 minus 22 is 42.
Now add the two answers. 67 plus 42 is 109.
So the sum is 109.
When you count along a list, the jumps are always one fewer than the position.
Three steps: find the greatest 2 digit prime, square it, and then find what the 4 in the answer is worth.

ask.ifNot: 99 can be divided by 9, and 93 by 3. 97 cannot be divided by anything, so it is the greatest 2 digit prime.

beats.say: Which is the greatest 2 digit prime?
So we must square 97. That means 97 times 97.
97 is 3 less than 100. So take 97 hundreds, 9700, and take away 3 lots of 97, which is 291. That leaves 9409.
So the square is 9409. Now find the 4.
Units, tens, hundreds. The 4 is in the hundreds place, so it is worth 4 times 100, which is 400.
So the place value of the 4 is 400.
Find the number, do the sum, then read the place. Take one step at a time and a long question becomes easy.

board.text: 2-digit primes with digit sum more than 10

beats.say: We go through the 2 digit primes and keep the ones whose digits add up to more than 10.

board.text: digit sum must be 11 or more

beats.say: More than 10 means 11 or bigger. Keep that in mind.
Small primes have small digit sums, so the first ones that pass are these. 29 gives 11, 47 gives 11, 59 gives 14 and 67 gives 13.
Carrying on: 79 gives 16, 83 gives 11, 89 gives 17 and 97 gives 16.

ask.ifNot: The question says more than 10. A sum of exactly 10 is not more than 10, so these three stay out.

beats.say: What about 19, 37 and 73? Each has a digit sum of exactly 10. Do they count?
So cross them out. This is the trap in the question.
Count the ones we kept: 4 in the first row and 4 in the second. That makes 8.
So there are 8 such primes. Read the words 'more than' carefully: they shut the door on exactly 10.
We want every one digit factor of 72, added together. A factor of 72 is a number that divides 72 exactly.
Test each one digit number, 1 to 9.

ask.ifNot: 9 times 8 is 72. So 9 is a factor, and so is its partner 8.

beats.say: Does 9 divide 72?
72 does not end in 0 or 5, so 5 is out. And 72 is not in the 7 times table, so 7 is out. Everything else divides 72.
Now add the ones left: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 9. Make it easy. 1 and 9 are 10, 2 and 8 are 10. That is 20.
Then 3, 4 and 6 make 13. And 20 plus 13 is 33.
So the sum is 33.
List, test, cross out, then add in friendly pairs that make 10.
A recipe with three steps: add, multiply, then look at the hundreds place of the answer.
The one digit odd numbers are 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9. Together they make 25.

ask.ifNot: 99 can be divided by 9, and 95 by 5. 97 cannot be divided by anything, so it is the one.

beats.say: And which is the greatest 2 digit prime?
So we need 25 times 97. 97 is 3 less than 100. 25 hundreds is 2500. Take away 25 threes, which is 75, and we get 2425.
Now the hundreds place of 2425. Units, tens, hundreds: the digit there is 4.
4 hundreds: 4 times 100 is 400.
So the place value of the hundreds digit is 400.
Careful with the last step: the question wants the place value, 400, and not just the digit 4.
Two hunts and then an addition: the 12th even number after 99, and the 18th even number before 99.
Start with the even numbers after 99. The first one is 100, and they go up in jumps of 2.

ask.ifNot: The 1st needs no jump at all. So the 12th needs one fewer than 12, which is 11 jumps.

beats.say: 100 is the 1st. How many jumps of 2 take us to the 12th?
11 jumps of 2 is 22. And 100 plus 22 is 122.
Now go backwards from 99. The first even number before it is 98. For the 18th we need 17 jumps back.
17 jumps of 2 is 34. And 98 minus 34 is 64.
Add the two: 122 plus 64 is 186.
So the sum is 186. The 1st one costs no jumps, so always use one fewer jump than the position.

board.text: six hundred hundreds = how many tens?

beats.say: Six hundred hundreds. That sounds like a tongue twister, so let's turn it into numbers.

ask.ifNot: Times 100 puts 2 more zeros on the end. 600 with 2 more zeros is 60,000.

beats.say: Six hundred is 600, and one hundred is 100. So six hundred hundreds means 600 lots of 100. What is 600 times 100?
600 times 100 is 60,000. Two more zeros on the end.

ask.ifNot: Each ten is a group of 10. To see how many groups of 10 fit into a number, we divide it by 10.

beats.say: Careful: 60,000 is the whole amount, not the number of tens. How do we find how many tens are inside it?
Dividing by 10 takes one zero off the end. 60,000 becomes 6000.
Check by going back: 6000 tens is 6000 times 10, which is 60,000. That is our six hundred hundreds.
So 6000 tens form six hundred hundreds. Turn the words into a number first, then ask how many tens fit in.

board.text: place value = face value, in every place?

beats.say: We want a digit whose place value and face value are the same, wherever it sits. Face value is the digit as it looks. Place value is what it is worth in its column.
Let's test 9. Put it in the tens place. Now it is worth 9 times 10, which is 90, but its face is still 9. Not the same.

ask.ifNot: 1 in the tens column means one ten. That is worth 10, not 1.

beats.say: Now try 1 in the tens place. Is its place value the same as its face value?
1 in the tens place is worth 10, but its face value is 1. So 1 does not work either.
Now zero. Put 0 in the tens place, the hundreds place, the thousands place. 0 times 10 is 0. 0 times 100 is 0. 0 times 1000 is 0.
Zero times anything is zero. So the place value of 0 is always 0, and its face value is 0 as well. They match in every column.
So the digit is 0.
In the units place every digit matches its face value. But only zero keeps them equal everywhere.

board.text: The place value is odd. Which place?

beats.say: A digit has an odd place value. Which column could it be sitting in? Let's try a digit, say 7, in different columns and see.

ask.ifNot: 70 ends in 0, and any number ending in 0 can be halved exactly. So it is even.

beats.say: In the tens place, 7 is worth 7 times 10, which is 70. Is 70 odd or even?
Even. In fact anything times 10 ends in 0, so a place value in the tens column is always even.
Hundreds and thousands tell the same story. 700 and 7000 both end in zeros, so they are even too.
But in the units place, 7 is worth just 7. No zero on the end, and 7 is odd.
Careful: the digit itself must be odd too. A 4 in the units place is worth 4, which is even. But the units place is the only one where odd is possible at all.
So a digit with an odd place value must be in the units place.
Tens, hundreds and beyond always end in zero, so they are always even. Odd place values live only in the units place.
Here is 69512. We need two special digits: the one with the greatest place value, and the one with the least.
Place value depends on the column. The column furthest left is worth the most, and the column furthest right is worth the least.

ask.ifNot: 9 is the biggest digit to look at, but it sits in the thousands. The 6 is in the ten-thousands, so the 6 is worth more.

beats.say: So which digit has the greatest place value?
The 6 is worth 60000. The 9 is only worth 9000. Don't let the big 9 fool you.
And the least place value is in the units column. That is the 2, worth just 2.
The question asks for the difference between the digits themselves. 6 minus 2 is 4.
So the difference is 4.
Greatest place value means furthest left. Least means furthest right. The size of the digit does not decide it.
Here is 76025. We are comparing the place value of the 6 with the place value of the 2.

ask.ifNot: Count the columns from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands. So the 6 means 6 thousands.

beats.say: Here they are in the chart. The 6 sits in the thousands column. What is it worth?
6 times 1000 is 6000. And the 2 is in the tens column, so it is worth 2 times 10, which is 20.

ask.ifNot: Dividing the digits, 6 by 2, forgets their columns. We must divide the place values: 6000 by 20.

beats.say: Now, how many times 20 is 6000? Which sum tells us?
6000 divided by 20. Cross one zero off each to make it easy: 600 divided by 2 is 300.
Check it: 300 times 20 gives back 6000. It works.
So the place value of the 6 is 300 times the place value of the 2.
Two place values first, then one division. Dividing the digits alone would have given 3, and missed by a long way.
Four numbers, each with two 8s. In just one of them, one 8 is worth a thousand times the other 8.

ask.ifNot: Each column is one more times 10. We need times 10 three times over to reach 1000, so the 8s are 3 columns apart.

beats.say: Here is the key. Each step to the left makes a digit worth 10 times more, and 10 times 10 times 10 is 1000. So how far apart must the two 8s be?
So we just hunt for two 8s that are 3 columns apart. In 68815 the 8s are side by side, only 1 apart. Out.
65818 has one 8 in the hundreds and one in the units. That is 2 apart. Out.
81586 has one 8 in the ten-thousands and one in the tens. Count the steps between them: 3. This looks right!
Check with the real values. The first 8 is worth 80000 and the other is worth 80. 80000 divided by 80 is 1000.
And in 85168 the 8s are 4 apart, which would be ten thousand times. So that one is out too.
So the number is 81586. The digit is the same both times, so only the gap between the columns matters.
Four numbers, and each has more than one 3. We want the one where one 3 is worth a hundred times another 3.

ask.ifNot: One step left is times 10. Two steps is times 10 and times 10 again, which is times 100. So 2 columns apart.

beats.say: Each column to the left is worth 10 times more, and 10 times 10 is 100. So how far apart must the 3s be?
134639: its 3s are in the ten-thousands and the tens. That is 3 apart. Too far.
752339: the two 3s are next door to each other. Only 1 apart.
863135: one 3 in the thousands, one in the tens. 2 apart. Promising!
Check with the values. The first 3 is worth 3000, the other is worth 30. 3000 divided by 30 is 100.
And 307638 has one 3 in the lakhs place and one in the tens, 4 apart. Out.
So the number is 863135. To be 100 times bigger, the same digit must sit exactly 2 columns to the left.

board.text: digits 1, 5, 0, 8: greatest number, then its successor

beats.say: Two jobs here. First build the greatest number from the digits 1, 5, 0 and 8. Then find its successor.

ask.ifNot: The thousands place is worth the most, so it deserves the biggest digit we have. That is 8.

beats.say: For the greatest number, the biggest digit should go where it is worth the most: the thousands place. Which digit goes first?
Then the next biggest in the hundreds, and so on down: 8, 5, 1, 0. That gives 8510.
Now, successor. That is simply the number that comes next when we count. So we add 1.
Careful: the successor does not have to use our four digits. 8511 has two 1s, and that is fine. It is just the next number.
So the answer is 8511.
Greatest number: biggest digits first. Successor: add 1. Two small steps.
We build the greatest odd number from 5, 8, 0, 7 and 4, and then look at its middle digit.

ask.ifNot: A number is odd when its units digit is odd. The other digits make no difference.

beats.say: Whether a number is odd is decided by one digit only. Which one?
So the last digit must be odd. Our odd digits are 5 and 7.

ask.ifNot: The units place is worth the least. So we give it the smaller odd digit, 5, and keep the 7 for a place that is worth more.

beats.say: We want the number as big as possible. So which odd digit should we spend on the units place?
With 5 at the end, arrange the rest from biggest to smallest: 8, 7, 4, 0. That makes 87405.
Compare it with putting 7 last, which gives 85407. That is smaller, so 87405 wins.
Now the middle. There are 5 digits, so the middle one is the third: 4.
Decide the last digit first, using the smaller odd digit. Then line the others up, biggest first.
First we build the smallest even number from 2, 7, 3, 9 and 6. Then we find what its 7 is worth.
Even means the last digit is even. Our even digits are 2 and 6, so one of them must go last.

ask.ifNot: The front place is worth the most, so the smallest digit should go there to keep the number small. That means the 6 goes last.

beats.say: For the smallest number, the 2 is precious. Where is it most useful?
So 6 goes at the end, and the others go from smallest to biggest: 2, 3, 7, 9. That makes 23796.
Check the other choice. Ending in 2, the smallest we could make is 36792, and that is bigger.
Now find the 7. Count from the right: units, tens, hundreds. The 7 is in the hundreds place.
7 hundreds: 7 times 100 is 700.
Careful: 'hundreds' is only the name of the place. The place value is the number, 700.
Build the number first, then read the place. Two questions hiding in one.

board.text: 2-digit even numbers with an odd tens digit

beats.say: We are counting 2 digit numbers that are even, and have an odd digit in the tens place. Let's count the choices for each place.
The tens digit must be odd: 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. That is 5 choices.

ask.ifNot: The even digits are 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8. Do not forget 0: it is even too. That makes 5.

beats.say: The number must be even, so the units digit is even. How many choices are there for it?
0, 2, 4, 6, 8. Five choices, and zero is one of them.
Each tens digit can pair with every one of those. Take tens digit 1: we get 10, 12, 14, 16, 18. That is 5 numbers.
The same happens for 3, 5, 7 and 9. So 5 tens digits, with 5 numbers each: 5 times 5 is 25.
So there are 25 such numbers.
Count the choices for each place, then multiply. No need to write out all 25.
Four digits, 7, 0, 3 and 9, each used once. How many different 4 digit numbers can we make? Let's fill the places one at a time, from the left.

ask.ifNot: 0 cannot go first, because then the number would really have only 3 digits. So only 7, 3 or 9 can lead. 3 choices.

beats.say: Start with the thousands place. How many of our digits are allowed there?
Zero cannot lead, so the thousands place has 3 choices.
One digit is used up, so 3 are left for the hundreds, and zero is welcome now. Then 2 are left for the tens, and 1 for the units.
Multiply the choices. 3 times 3 is 9, times 2 is 18, times 1 is still 18.
Let's check one group. Starting with 7 we get 7039, 7093, 7309, 7390, 7903 and 7930: 6 numbers. The same for 3 and for 9.
So 18 different numbers can be formed.
Go place by place from the left, count the choices, and multiply. Just remember that zero can never lead.
Digits 2, 5, 0 and 8, each used once. We want the 4 digit numbers that are less than 5000.

ask.ifNot: 0 cannot lead a 4 digit number. And with 5 in front the number is at least 5000, which is not less than 5000. Only 2 works.

beats.say: The thousands digit decides whether a number is below 5000. Which of our digits can go there?
So every one of our numbers starts with 2.
The digits 5, 0 and 8 fill the other three places. 3 choices for the hundreds, then 2 for the tens, then 1 for the units.
Six numbers, and even the biggest, 2850, is well below 5000.
So 6 numbers can be formed.
Deal with the place that has a rule first. Here that was the thousands place. Then count the rest and multiply.
Here is 469571. We are going to swap its 5 and its 6, and see how the number changes.
First, where are they? The 6 is in the ten-thousands place. The 5 is in the hundreds place.
Swap them. Now the 5 is in the ten-thousands place and the 6 is in the hundreds place: 459671.

ask.ifNot: Look at the ten-thousands place, the bigger of the two columns. It went down from 6 to 5. So the whole number went down.

beats.say: Before we subtract anything: is the new number bigger or smaller?
The ten-thousands place lost 1, so the number dropped by 10000. The hundreds place gained 1, so it rose by 100. Overall it fell by 9900.
Check by subtracting the whole numbers. 469571 minus 459671 is 9900.
So the new number is less by 9900.
When two digits swap, only their two columns change. The bigger column tells you whether the number went up or down.
A bundle of 5 rupee notes, numbered from 40801 to 40901. Two steps: count the notes, then multiply by 5.

ask.ifNot: Try it with small numbers. Notes 1 to 3 are 3 notes, but 3 minus 1 is only 2. We must add 1, to count the first note as well.

beats.say: So how many notes are there, from 40801 to 40901?
40901 minus 40801 is 100. Then add 1 for the first note, 40801 itself. That makes 101 notes.
This is the trap in the question. Subtracting counts the steps between the notes, and there is always one more note than steps.
Now the money. 100 notes of 5 rupees make 500 rupees, and 1 more note makes 505.
So the bundle holds 505 rupees.
Counting from one number to another: subtract, then add 1, because both ends are in the bundle.

board.text: primes from 1 to 100: how many 7s are written?

beats.say: Imagine writing out every prime number from 1 to 100. How many times would we write the digit 7? It can appear in the units place or in the tens place.
First, 7 in the units place. Here are all the numbers that end in 7. But not all of them are prime.

ask.ifNot: 27 is in the 3 times table, so it can be divided. 37 and 67 cannot be divided by anything.

beats.say: Which of these three is not a prime?
27, 57, 77 and 87 can all be divided, so they go. Six primes are left, and each has one 7.
Now 7 in the tens place: the seventies. The primes there are 71, 73 and 79. Three more 7s.
6 and 3 make 9.
So the digit 7 is written 9 times.
Sort the search by place: 7 in the units, then 7 in the tens. And 77, with its two 7s, never counted, because it is not prime.
Imagine writing out every 2 digit prime. How many times do we write the digit 3? Let's look at the units place first, then the tens place.
Here are all the 2 digit numbers ending in 3.

ask.ifNot: Add the digits of each. 3 plus 3, 6 plus 3 and 9 plus 3 are all multiples of 3. So 33, 63 and 93 can be divided by 3.

beats.say: Three of these are in the 3 times table, so they are not prime. Which three?
Cross them out. Six primes are left: 13, 23, 43, 53, 73 and 83. That is six 3s.
Next, 3 in the tens place: the thirties. The primes there are 31 and 37. Two more 3s.
6 and 2 make 8. And 33, the only number with two 3s, is not prime, so nothing was counted twice.
So the digit 3 is written 8 times.
Split the search by place, units then tens, and throw out anything that is not prime.

board.text: all 1-digit primes, each once: how many even numbers?

beats.say: We use all the one digit primes, each exactly once, and count the even numbers we can make.

ask.ifNot: 1 is not a prime, and 9 is 3 times 3. But 2 is a prime, the only even one. So the list is 2, 3, 5, 7.

beats.say: First we need the one digit primes. Which list is right?
Four digits, and all of them are used. So every number we make has 4 digits.
An even number must end in an even digit. Only 2 is even, so 2 is locked into the units place.
That leaves 3, 5 and 7 for the other three places. 3 choices, then 2, then 1.
Here they all are: 3572, 3752, 5372, 5732, 7352, 7532. Every one ends in 2.
So 6 even numbers can be formed.
Fix the place that has a rule first. Then count the choices for the rest and multiply.

board.text: From 1 to 201: how many are divisible by 8?

beats.say: We are counting the numbers from 1 to 201 that 8 divides exactly, with nothing left over.
Divisible by 8 means the number is in the 8 times table. So really, we are counting multiples of 8.

ask.ifNot: 208 is past 201, and 192 is not the last one we can reach. The last multiple of 8 inside the range is 200.

beats.say: Let's find the far end first. Which is the last multiple of 8 that does not go past 201?
8 times 25 is 200. One more step gives 208, and that is past 201.
Look at the 8 times table from its very start. 200 is multiple number 25. So up to 201 there are 25 multiples of 8.
Do we lose any at the start? No. Our range begins at 1, and the first multiple, 8, is already inside. All 25 count.
Check another way. From 8 to 200 is 192. That is 24 jumps of 8, and 24 jumps join 25 numbers.
So 25 numbers from 1 to 201 are divisible by 8.
When the range starts at 1, just find the last multiple and see which number it is in the times table.

board.text: A book has 50 pages. How many digits?

beats.say: A book with 50 pages. Every page has its number printed on it, and we are counting all the digits in those numbers.
Careful: this is not the same as counting pages. Page 5 uses 1 digit, but page 50 uses 2.

ask.ifNot: Page 10 already needs 2 digits, a 1 and a 0. And there is no page 0. So the 1 digit pages are 1 to 9.

beats.say: So we sort the pages by how many digits they use. Which pages use just 1 digit?
That is 9 pages with 1 digit each. 9 digits so far.

ask.ifNot: Take away the 9 pages we have already counted. 50 minus 9 leaves 41.

beats.say: Next come the 2 digit pages, from 10 up to 50. How many pages is that?
50 minus 9 is 41 pages. Each has 2 digits, so 41 times 2 is 82 digits.
Now add up the digits: 9 plus 82 makes 91.
So numbering all 50 pages takes 91 digits.
Group the pages by the length of their numbers, work out each group, and add them up. That works for any book.
How many 3-digit even numbers are there? Far too many to list, so we will count them cleverly.

ask.ifNot: 99 has only 2 digits. One more than that is 100, the very first number with 3 digits.

beats.say: First, the smallest 3-digit number. What is it?
And the largest is 999, because one more makes 1000, and that needs 4 digits.
Now count. From 1 up to 999 there are 999 numbers. But 1 to 99 are too short, so we take those 99 away. 900 are left.

ask.ifNot: The list starts at 100, which is even, and ends at 999, which is odd. So they pair up neatly, one even and one odd in every pair. Half are even.

beats.say: Now, how many of these 900 are even? Think of them in order: even, odd, even, odd. They take turns.
Pair them up: 100 with 101, 102 with 103, all the way to 998 with 999. Each pair has one even number. So 900 divided by 2 is 450.
Check it place by place. 9 choices for the first digit, 10 for each middle place, and only 5 for the last digit, which must be even. That gives 450 again.
So the count of 3-digit even numbers is 450.
Count them all first, then halve, because even and odd numbers take turns.

board.text: From 50 to 100: how many are divisible by 6?

beats.say: From 50 to 100, some numbers can be divided by 6 exactly. Our job is to count them.
Divisible by 6 means the number is in the 6 times table. So really, we are counting multiples of 6.

ask.ifNot: 102 is past 100, and 90 is not the last one we can reach. The last multiple of 6 inside the range is 96.

beats.say: Let's find the far end first. Which is the last multiple of 6 that does not go past 100?
6 times 16 is 96. One more step gives 102, and that is past 100.
Look at the 6 times table from its very start. 96 is multiple number 16. So up to 100 there are 16 multiples of 6.
But our range only starts at 50. 6 times 8 is 48, still too small. The next one, 54, is the first one inside.

ask.ifNot: The too small ones run up to 48, and 48 is 6 times 8. So exactly 8 of them go.

beats.say: So out of the 16 multiples, how many are too small and have to go?
So we take 8 away from 16, and 8 are left.
Check by listing them: 54, 60, 66, 72, 78, 84, 90, 96. Count them, and there are 8.
So 8 numbers from 50 to 100 are divisible by 6.
The plan: find the last multiple, count from the start of the table, then take away the ones that are too small.

board.text: A book has 100 pages. How many digits?

beats.say: A book with 100 pages. Every page has its number printed on it, and we are counting all the digits in those numbers.
Careful: this is not the same as counting pages. Page 5 uses 1 digit, but page 100 uses 3.

ask.ifNot: Page 10 already needs 2 digits, a 1 and a 0. And there is no page 0. So the 1 digit pages are 1 to 9.

beats.say: So we sort the pages by how many digits they use. Which pages use just 1 digit?
That is 9 pages with 1 digit each. 9 digits so far.

ask.ifNot: From 1 to 99 there are 99 pages. Take away the 9 we have already counted, and 90 are left.

beats.say: Next come the 2 digit pages, from 10 up to 99. How many pages is that?
99 minus 9 is 90 pages. Each has 2 digits, so 90 times 2 is 180 digits.
Last comes page 100, the only page with 3 digits. Take away the first 99 pages and just 1 is left.
1 page with 3 digits is 3 more digits.
Now add up all the digits: 9 plus 180 plus 3 makes 192.
So numbering all 100 pages takes 192 digits.
The plan: sort the pages by how many digits they have, count each group, then add.
How many 3-digit numbers are there? Far too many to list, so we will count them cleverly.

ask.ifNot: 99 has only 2 digits. One more than that is 100, the very first number with 3 digits.

beats.say: First, the smallest 3-digit number. What is it?
And the largest is 999, because one more makes 1000, and that needs 4 digits.
Now count. From 1 up to 999 there are 999 numbers. But 1 to 99 are too short, so we take those 99 away. 900 are left.
Check it place by place. The first digit can be 1 to 9, never 0, so 9 choices. Every other place can be 0 to 9, so 10 choices. Multiply, and we get 900 again.
So the count of 3-digit numbers is 900.
Smallest, largest, then take away the ones that are too short. Or count the choices for each place and multiply.

board.text: From 100 to 300: how many are divisible by 5?

beats.say: From 100 to 300, some numbers can be divided by 5 exactly. Our job is to count them.
Divisible by 5 means the number is in the 5 times table. So really, we are counting multiples of 5.

ask.ifNot: 300 itself is in the 5 times table, and it is inside our range. So 300 is the last one.

beats.say: Let's find the far end first. Which is the last multiple of 5 that does not go past 300?
5 times 60 is exactly 300. It lands right on the end of our range, so it counts.
Look at the 5 times table from its very start. 300 is multiple number 60. So up to 300 there are 60 multiples of 5.
Careful here: 100 itself is in the 5 times table, so it counts. The ones that are too small stop at 95, which is 5 times 19.

ask.ifNot: The too small ones run up to 95, and 95 is 5 times 19. So exactly 19 of them go.

beats.say: So out of the 60 multiples, how many are too small and have to go?
So we take 19 away from 60, and 41 are left.
Check another way. From 100 to 300 is 200. That is 40 jumps of 5, and 40 jumps join 41 numbers.
So 41 numbers from 100 to 300 are divisible by 5.
The plan: find the last multiple, count from the start of the table, then take away the ones that are too small.

board.text: A book has 150 pages. How many digits?

beats.say: A book with 150 pages. Every page has its number printed on it, and we are counting all the digits in those numbers.
Careful: this is not the same as counting pages. Page 5 uses 1 digit, but page 150 uses 3.

ask.ifNot: Page 10 already needs 2 digits, a 1 and a 0. And there is no page 0. So the 1 digit pages are 1 to 9.

beats.say: So we sort the pages by how many digits they use. Which pages use just 1 digit?
That is 9 pages with 1 digit each. 9 digits so far.

ask.ifNot: From 1 to 99 there are 99 pages. Take away the 9 we have already counted, and 90 are left.

beats.say: Next come the 2 digit pages, from 10 up to 99. How many pages is that?
99 minus 9 is 90 pages. Each has 2 digits, so 90 times 2 is 180 digits.
Last come the 3 digit pages, 100 up to 150. Take away the first 99 pages: 150 minus 99 leaves 51 pages.
51 pages with 3 digits each: 51 times 3 is 153 digits.
Now add up all the digits: 9 plus 180 plus 153 makes 342.
So numbering all 150 pages takes 342 digits.
The plan: sort the pages by how many digits they have, count each group, then add.
How many 2-digit even numbers are there? Far too many to list, so we will count them cleverly.

ask.ifNot: 9 has only 1 digit. One more than that is 10, the very first number with 2 digits.

beats.say: First, the smallest 2-digit number. What is it?
And the largest is 99, because one more makes 100, and that needs 3 digits.
Now count. From 1 up to 99 there are 99 numbers. But 1 to 9 are too short, so we take those 9 away. 90 are left.

ask.ifNot: The list starts at 10, which is even, and ends at 99, which is odd. So they pair up neatly, one even and one odd in every pair. Half are even.

beats.say: Now, how many of these 90 are even? Think of them in order: even, odd, even, odd. They take turns.
Pair them up: 10 with 11, 12 with 13, all the way to 98 with 99. Each pair has one even number. So 90 divided by 2 is 45.
Check it place by place. 9 choices for the tens digit, because it cannot be 0. And only 5 for the units digit, which must be even. 9 times 5 is 45.
So the count of 2-digit even numbers is 45.
Count them all first, then halve, because even and odd numbers take turns.

board.text: From 10 to 210: how many are divisible by 9?

beats.say: From 10 to 210, some numbers can be divided by 9 exactly. Our job is to count them.
Divisible by 9 means the number is in the 9 times table. So really, we are counting multiples of 9.

ask.ifNot: 216 is past 210, and 198 is not the last one we can reach. The last multiple of 9 inside the range is 207.

beats.say: Start at the top end. What is the biggest multiple of 9 that is not more than 210?
9 times 23 is 207. One more step gives 216, and that is past 210.
Look at the 9 times table from its very start. 207 is multiple number 23. So up to 210 there are 23 multiples of 9.
But our range only starts at 10. 9 times 1 is 9, still too small. The next one, 18, is the first one inside.

ask.ifNot: The too small ones run up to 9, and 9 is 9 times 1. So exactly 1 of them go.

beats.say: So out of the 23 multiples, how many are too small and have to go?
23 take away 1 leaves 22.
Check another way. From 18 to 207 is 189. That is 21 jumps of 9, and 21 jumps join 22 numbers.
So 22 numbers from 10 to 210 are divisible by 9.
The plan: find the last multiple, count from the start of the table, then take away the ones that are too small.

board.text: A book has 200 pages. How many digits?

beats.say: A book with 200 pages. Every page has its number printed on it, and we are counting all the digits in those numbers.
Careful: this is not the same as counting pages. Page 5 uses 1 digit, but page 200 uses 3.

ask.ifNot: Page 10 already needs 2 digits, a 1 and a 0. And there is no page 0. So the 1 digit pages are 1 to 9.

beats.say: So we sort the pages by how many digits they use. Which pages use just 1 digit?
That is 9 pages with 1 digit each. 9 digits so far.

ask.ifNot: From 1 to 99 there are 99 pages. Take away the 9 we have already counted, and 90 are left.

beats.say: Next come the 2 digit pages, from 10 up to 99. How many pages is that?
99 minus 9 is 90 pages. Each has 2 digits, so 90 times 2 is 180 digits.
Last come the 3 digit pages, 100 up to 200. Take away the first 99 pages: 200 minus 99 leaves 101 pages.
101 pages with 3 digits each: 101 times 3 is 303 digits.
Now add up all the digits: 9 plus 180 plus 303 makes 492.
So numbering all 200 pages takes 492 digits.
Group the pages by the length of their numbers, work out each group, and add them up. That works for any book.

board.text: Odd numbers from 100 to 140: how many?

beats.say: From 100 to 140, how many of the numbers are odd? Let's count them without writing every one.

ask.ifNot: 100 is even, so it does not count. The very next number, 101, is the first odd one.

beats.say: Where does our list start? Which is the first odd number in the range?
So we start at 101. And the last one is 139, because 140 is even.
Odd numbers go up in jumps of 2: 101, 103, 105 and so on, all the way to 139.
From 101 to 139 is 38. Each jump is 2, so that is 19 jumps.

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3. There is always one more number than jumps.

beats.say: 19 jumps. So how many numbers are on our list?
One more than the jumps: 19 plus 1 is 20. That extra 1 is our starting number.
